UBS Asia S&T desk update

Korean Memory Selling Intensifies; Buying In TSMC, Japan Industrials; Financials Lack Bid

Japan surprisingly constructive: Overall flows are modestly net bought despite the sharp market selloff, with Japan dominating early regional turnover. The bid is concentrated in industrials, particularly automation and selected diversified capital goods, rather than generic dip-buying.

Japanese technology also finding buyers: Outside memory, where Kioxia remains less convincing, technology hardware has turned net bought after being 2:1 sold Thursday. AI hardware and semiconductor equipment names are seeing demand into weakness, suggesting selective bottom-fishing rather than wholesale tech capitulation.

Korea shows the clearest capitulation: Selling remains acute in both SK Hynix (4:1 better to sell) and Samsung Electronics (5:1 better to sell). Taiwan is less extreme, with meaningful support from long-only investors in TSMC helping absorb supply and stem broader outflows.

Little evidence of a classic defensive rotation: Consumer staples are modestly better bought but represent a very small share of desk flows. More importantly, financials are failing to attract defensive flows, with Japanese banks and insurers heavily offered and Hong Kong/China insurers also seeing broad outflows. AIA is the notable exception. Australian banks are the relative refuge, while Singapore bank flows remain mixed.

China’s domestic semiconductors remain differentiated: Selected domestic chip names continue to attract buying despite the regional rout. CXMT is the exception, failing to participate in the domestic bid and seeing outflows that are more consistent with the weakness across Korean and Japanese memory.

This week's results make me optimistic. We have an unprecedented bipartisan opportunity to take on Big Tech’s abuse of market power and open up markets for the next generation of founders.

Inventing powerful AI is only half the job. People must be able to use it to make their lives better and their businesses more productive. That gets harder when a few trillion-dollar companies can block new products from reaching them.

Congress can open those markets for Little Tech. Let thousands of startups compete to lower costs and grow the economy for everyone. We should spread the gains from AI as widely as possible, not concentrate even more power in the companies that already control distribution.

A departure from my usual gloating:

If you lost all your money today, I'm sorry that happened. However you must understand that it was deserved. It means you had critical leaks in your trading and you need to take a break. Days like this happen infrequently but they will continue to happen for entirety of your trading career. 

Being levered is reserved for only the specialist of situations, you should almost never leverage. Never allow yourself to be in the position of a forced seller.

If you're having dark thoughts, or feel like you've taken 10 steps backwards and want to do something drastic, please don't. Life is far longer and opportunities are abundant.

Do not trade anytime soon. Go back and reflect on what your leak was (risk management, sloppy order placement, etc.) and learn. You paid your tuition.

If you continue trading without being self critical you are not a trader you are a PROBLEM GAMBLER.

Investing, trading and the journey to becoming wealthy rarely happens overnight. The only way to become profitable is to become your own harshest critic.

tweets.text:
7 new things you should know about how ChatGPT searches for info (that will help your site optimization) ↓

1️⃣ ChatGPT now runs more fan-out searches per prompt, and the free and cheaper tiers are catching up to higher-tier models.

Fan-out means the AI autonomously rewrites your single question into multiple, hyper-specific sub-queries.

You ask: "What are the top gyms in Dubai?"
ChatGPT will search:

• Search 1: "top gyms Dubai 2026 reviews"
• Search 2: "Dubai gyms pricing comparison"
• Search 3: "site:https://t.co/H2MThwXEl9 best gym Dubai"

2️⃣ Being named in ChatGPT's first fan-out query drives a much higher chance of being cited: brands mentioned there were cited 68.9% of the time, versus just 2.1% for pages that were only fetched.

3️⃣ The number of unique domains cited per ChatGPT response dropped from 19 to 15 after the 5.3 update, even as more pages are retrieved.

4️⃣ Product pages now make up 16.39% of retrieved pages in ChatGPT fan-out queries, overtaking listicles.

5️⃣ For facts, ChatGPT fan-out queries go to official brand sites. For opinions and product reviews, they favor reddit and review platforms.

6️⃣ 21 of 27 ChatGPT initial queries contained brand names never mentioned by the user.

7️⃣ ChatGPT sometimes guesses the wrong brand domain, directing site: queries at parked or unowned domains, especially for lesser-known brands.

Practitioner notes based on the above:

1. Trying to create content to target individual fan-out queries is not a good strategy and can land you in Google's spam filters.

2. Monitor your site's impressions in search console tools to understand how often fan-out queries are reaching your site.

3. If your brand shares a name with other businesses or domains, consider adding 'Official Site' to your title or meta description to help ChatGPT and users identify the right site.

4. Make sure your key facts are in plain HTML on your brand's domain so ChatGPT can retrieve them via site: searches.

S/o to @lilyraynyc for this data; originally shared on Substack ↓
https://t.co/G0vRSFxibP

$AAOI earnings:

- $1B-$1.5B LTA disclosed with a hyperscaler customer

- 2nd LTA coming soon, worth 5x+ more (implying $5B-$7.5B), in its final stages. 

This LTA explicitly includes lasers, very material for AOI that they're moving to supplying merchant lasers. 

- "The demand is exceptional, unprecedented. I do not know what kind of superlatives to use to describe the amount of demand that we are seeing out there in the industry"

Yeah this commentary doesn't sound like any optical demand would slowed down if it's "exceptional + unprecedented" 

- Rejected hyperscaler slowdowns from political changes with little effect. 

- AOI Can only meet 80% of demand, in case there's a kind of reduction, the demand would be bigger than AOI future capacity

- Moving toward other financing methods than ATMs (thank god), US bank loans similar to what $NBIS is doing, I'd argue is positive, given FCF coming in later. 

- Delay in meeting capacity projections into H1 2027. $471m/month targets pushed back into H2 2027, due to electrical procurement and construction logistics, which existed before Texas governor changed. 

This part is negative part of the earnings call. To qualify this, I don't quite think hyperscalers would sign a $5-$7.5B LTA if they didn't think AOI couldn't deliver.

-  Near term Q4 guidance cut was DSP availability. AOI revised near term projections down slightly to $385M and $420M in revenue. 

Said DSP supply would ease early 2027 and that they're qualifying more suppliers. 

- Gave hiked H2 2027 capacity projections from their expansion, near term revision downward. 

- 4 to 5 ongoing UHP laser eval/quals for CPO

UHP laser segment alone would far outweigh their $3.8B MC, especially if you're executing on multi billion dollar contracts with 60%+ gross margin laseres.

TLDR:
- Long term visibility improved a lot, with est. $6-$9B cumulative LTA contracts coming soon. 
- Shift toward supplying CPO lasers merchant is fundamentally material vs. just transceivers, and what I wanted to hear
- Capacity guidance hiked into H2 2027, near term delays from electrical/DSP related procurement + installation.  

I still think we're reached peak fear levels, but wouldn't dismiss disappointing short term procurement delays + Q4 DSP bottlenecks. 

AOI likely signing an additional +$5-$7.5B in likely hyperscaler LTAs and entering merchant UHP CPO market dominanted by $LITE + $COHR. 

Factored in with the valuation drop has made medium-long term opportunities very compelling.

i mean, there's very good reasons why you can't build them offshore. 

latency, for one. many uses of AI are incompatible with 120 ms of ping. DCs need to be near population centers. especially if youre doing real time voice stuff. 

cheap energy doesn't mean sufficiently abundant. none of those countries you mentioned have the capacity to support 100 GW of incremental demand (the three countries you mention account for 100 GW in total, altogether). you're not doubling their grids in 3 years. not possible. 

more importantly, governance. El Salvador is a quasi dictatorship. Chile is a former dictatorship. Poland is in the midst of a coup. to build durable infrastructure – especially energy, which must last for decades – you have to believe in multiple decades of stable governance and respect for property rights. 

there's nothing wrong with those countries per se, but there's no country on earth besides the US that has the following characteristics: 

- abundant energy, and the ability to further grow the grid
- a local population base that is willing to bear the massive fixed costs of expanding the grid 
- a relatively permissive approach to actually building things (mostly in red states)
- a genuine respect for property rights
- functional governance and the rule of law
- local demand for compute
- deep and liquid capital markets 

China satisfies some of those criteria, but obviously the US cannot build its data centers there. 

there's a reason the data center by capacity chart looks the way it does.

As funny as this headline is, there's a reason for it.

They kept the nuclear systems on this tech until like 2019. The FAA is phasing out now.

Super-secure slow-update tech like nuclear, air traffic, or banking, doesn't want to touch the outside world for as long as possible.

Given all this recent AI hacking news, you likely understand what I'm saying better than if I said it a year ago.

When existential systems are updated, it requires extreme vetting. Old tech is sometimes good, actually, if it's isolated and maintained as critical. https://t.co/nOt1Ni8gNH

Source: I worked for 12 years at the FAA in their simulation division for new technology.

The FAA isn't perfect, but much like the nuclear arsenal and major bank backups, you absolutely want to minimize overhauling the core system until you absolutely have to.

@HodlMagoo That's only partially true.

But it's also bureaucracy, funding, and risk mitigation. It takes decisiveness to change a system that's working.

The fact is tons of highly energized smart people were involved, but had to navigate around the existing context of a critical system.

@HodlMagoo It's similar to why nuclear generation sites don't have a ton of frequent updates.

Security over progress. Maintenance over innovation.

Not laziness, per se.

@SantiagoAuFund Exactly.

Bitcoin Core maintainers and hardware designers have to build with that intention in mind.

There's even a meme now that like people who bought 2010s-era hardware wallets and never updated are literally winning vs current hacks. Chad stuck with his tech.

I'm happy to be partnering with @mezzanine_fi to bring a bit of attention to their protocol, because I think they're trying something interesting here

In simple terms, most DeFi vaults treat everyone the same. Everyone earns the same yield, and if something goes wrong everyone takes the same hit.

Mezzanine splits each vault into two sides:

Junior: which takes any losses first if the strategy loses money, in return for a higher yield for taking the risk

Senior: which earns a smaller share of the yield but only takes a loss once Junior has been wiped out, so it has some added downside coverage

Losses can still happen of course, but this allows depositors to have more customization in their risk/reward level while not changing the underlying strategy of the vault

My current strategy is just to use the Senior pool and take the modest (but still good) yield, mostly b/c i'm at a point where I don't want or need to be taking on additional risks with my stables and am content with 8-9% yield.

Where does the yield come from? Always the right question to ask. The yield in their first vault comes from real-world loans, home equity and car loans made through Figure (via Hastra) which is then looped to boost it.

The full chain is: people take out home or car loans through Figure, a big US fintech company that makes loans. Hastra brings Figure's loan interest into DeFi and turns the interest into tokens, Mezzanine borrows against those tokens on Morpho and Kamino to earn more, and then splits the result between Senior and Junior.

Right now the app shows 8.5% APY for Senior and 20.7% for Junior, though that moves week to week

As always NFA/DYOR, but imo it's worth checking out.

You can sign up here: https://t.co/VFXsBPpv9b

The market is still up meaningfully this year and has been on a ripper for the last few. So now is an important time to ask yourself: 

Are you nervous about your portfolio right now? If so, something is wrong:

- Do you have 6-12 months of expenses in savings?
- Are you spending more than you make?
- If you hold individual stocks, how correlated are they? Are they really one position? 
- What % of your net worth is your largest position? Is it too big? 
- Be honest: have you lived through a large drawdown before? How well do you know yourself? Will you panic? How do you know? How do you really know?

For some people these questions might seem silly. But I guess my account is pretty big now and if I can get some people to honestly reflect on how they’re positioned while the market is still up a lot I think that’s worth doing

This is not a market call. I have no idea what the market will do. This is about good financial hygiene so you don’t panic and do something stupid.

hearing some chatter that anthropic is now lowering down to $1tn to get this IPO done. let me explain why this doesnt matter and its actually all over-

the entire existence of this company is based on a funding model that inherently has extreme asset liability mismatch. what that means is that just like the hyperscalers are diluting their equity fund capex, there is an expectation that anthropic will also have to do the same. ie it needs strong equity to perpetuate the scheme

but if you IPO at the wrong price (and dont get a pop which increasingly appears they wont be; spacex already below) then youre now in the death spiral that crypto investors should be very familiar with: its called the reflexivity trap of the confidence game. its the "ill bid FTT at $22 all day" or the "steady lads UST is $1" game, with all its lucid horrors. and here is the key insight- the confidence game exists at the service of the creditors. if there is no credit, there is simply no equity. and there is no credit, if there is no collateral

if the credit rating agencies are not going to give IG at $2tn, they are certaintly not going a better HY rating at $1tn. and there is no world in which anthropic can exist without credit because ~$1tn of commit, much of which is noncancellable, is a straight up negative equity pledge

yet there were two scenarios in which i was willing to concede anthropic could IPO: first 1) the improbable but possible was if the hyperscalers/chips oligopoly came to rescue and plug the hole, given their incestuous nature of revenue bookings and paper gains/losses at scale. but it is clear now that the market has spoken this will lead to a mutual death, and should not be attempted. or perversely even better, they are actually better off letting anthropic go to zero so they can acquire the pieces on the cheap which is the best nash equilibrium outcome, not just for the dominant player but for society at large. second 2) the us government can nationalize the company and collude with other sovereigns (like UAE, Saudi, Japan who are basically already the checks) to force its funding as a collective bargain. this gives you trillions, which is actually the most effective backstop to restore market confidence. the first edge case does require an IPO, but the second edge case here for which i believe there is still a good chance that this is the ultimate end game- will require a failed IPO to recapitalize at a normalized price for the consortium (and dont forget that openai front ran this investor group in anticipation of this dynamic to play out as a private co last month)

i believe the market is crapping out today because the market is recognizing it will not IPO. and actually, as ive said before, this is a very good thing. i might even imagine that the market could quickly rebound on the news of its IPO being delayed because it allows #2) to play out, as not only a national, but an international bailout. the US is more likely to tolerate, even relish, the taxes of foreginers to fund our domestic companies. that is the only end game that really matters, and the end game i am going to be excited to see

we'll see if this newly revamped washington can figure it out

thread_tweets.text:
This is one of the many reasons why market timing is so difficult.

When stocks plunge, the natural instinct is to sell and wait for things to calm down. And sometimes that's the right call in the short run, as additional declines follow.

But eventually, the market recovers. And those recoveries don't typically begin with a slow, gradual move higher. They often start with explosive rallies that catch investors completely off guard.

That's where market timing gets particularly difficult.

The investor who sold to avoid further losses suddenly faces another difficult decision: buy back at a higher price or wait for another correction that may never bring stocks back below their original selling price.

The problem with market timing isn't just knowing when to get out. You have to also know when to get back in.

And as history shows, some of the market's biggest gains occur when investors are least expecting them.

No one said this game was easy.

January 2025, post-Inauguration

“I was a ‘Never Trumper,’ and now I am rooting for him wholeheartedly to do great work.”

“He has to stay with the 2.0 agenda, as hard as it is, and stay away from the Steve Bannon agenda and the grifting. Those are the things that will take this all apart. So that's my appeal to them.”

March 2025, after Kristi Noem’s visit to a prison in El Salvador

“I believe that there is a sadistic nature to this administration. It is an Achilles' heel for them. And when you see them doing videos from these prisons and saying, ‘This is going to happen to you,’ this is why they will lose the midterms if they continue to do this type of stuff.”

October 2025, after Trump’s net approval hit a new low

“It's not pretty for Trump right now. Liberation Day when he did the tariffs, then the LA protests, remember the violent protests, and the ICE agents chasing people down in fields, not releasing the Epstein files in July. They don't like the chaos. The Democrats are going to shellack the Republicans in the midterms if this continues.”

November 2025, after inflation hit 3% in the September ‘25 print

“Trump sold people that prices would go down. We're back up to 3% inflation, folks. Not only is it not going down, it's going up. Trump has failed the middle class. That's the bottom line here.”

March 2026, after the US and Israel strike Iran, kicking off the war

“This is kind of the end of Trump's second term, and if you were to put together the series of mistakes that he's made, they're really at the heart of why people voted for him. You take starting a war like this, specifically with Iran, that's what we were told was the reason to vote for President Trump. He was not going to take us down this path. If this continues for another six months, it's basically going to result in the Democrats doing a clean sweep in the midterms.”

June 2026, after the Iran War exceeded initial timelines

“It’s just a huge, colossal error starting this Iran War, and hopefully we can get out of it. We can't be in a forever war, obviously.”

October 2026, on Midterm predictions

“All I have to say is, Trump promised not to start a war, he did. He promised to solve inflation, he didn't. The end. And I think the Democrats sweep.”

The blue wave has weighed on companies like ours. I get it. But let’s not confuse politics with long-term fundamentals.

Finance is moving onchain and demand for AI is exploding. These are generational shifts that will play out across administrations and market cycles.

We’ve spent years building Galaxy to win in both. That includes Texas, where we delivered Helios Phase I on schedule and 800 MW is already leased under long-term contract. We’ve worked with legislators and local communities there for years, and we’ll keep doing that with the new administration. We share the same goals: reliable power, protected water and strong communities.

I see a massive disconnect between where $GLXY trades and what I believe this company is worth. That’s why I’m buying more stock, starting today.

I’m betting on us, big time.

You fall and you fall hard. Some people won't get on the tightrope again, and some people will. And then they think, how to do that? How to be bold and aggressive and pull it off?

You start to think about doing things differently and practicing more. It is that combination of caution and practice that allows you to take it to limits that you never would have been able to take it to before. Once that is learned, everything changes, because it also teaches how to take the hits.

Getting banged up is fine, but getting knocked out of the game is not. The willingness to get banged but not knocked out of the game is a big part of that.
#RayDalio #Resilience #Principles

The market is treating a Dem sweep as an existential threat to AI infrastructure. It’s not.

Data centres can (and already are) being built outside the US. Hyperscalers have major footprints and active expansions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Canada and LatAm. Power, speed of permitting and cost drive site selection more than pure US policy.

If domestic buildouts slow, capital will simply reallocate. Global AI compute demand doesn’t disappear because Northern Virginia or Texas gets harder to permit. Latency-sensitive training prefers concentrated clusters, but inference, regional capacity and a large share of workloads work fine abroad.

The nutty part is the indiscriminate selling of the whole growth stock complex. High-quality, FCF-positive AI names and infrastructure software companies with multi-year visibility are getting lumped in with pure high-beta, negative-FCF builders that actually do have financing and execution risk. 

Policy friction in one country ≠ the end of the AI buildout.

International optionality is real.

Nasdaq-100 forward returns after one-day drops of 6.25% or more, like today’s (NDX, Jan 1985 to Nov 2026, n=33 days).

Takeaways:

➤ 21 days later: average +5.2% vs +1.3% for any day. Index higher in 64% of cases vs 63%.

➤ 63 days later: average +4.9% vs +4.1% for any day. Index higher in 64% of cases vs 69%. By 3 months the edge is mostly gone.

➤ Further losses common: NDX fell another 10% or more within 63 days in 21 of 33 cases.

➤ In 1987 and 2020 a fast policy backstop ended the forced selling within two weeks. In 2000–01 and 2008 earnings and credit losses that policy couldn’t fix kept the index falling for months.

Today’s trigger was the midterms. Texas elected Hinojosa as governor on a promise to freeze data center permits, and voters elsewhere passed restrictions in 40 of 41 local data center ballot measures.

The obvious comparison is 2000. But the 2000 crash came from collapsing demand, while this comes from expected policy changes, and expectations can reverse.

The closest precedent is April 2025: NDX fell 6.1% on tariffs, Trump hit pause three sessions later, and NDX was up 30.5% after 63 days. Then one person caused the shock and could reverse it. Here expectations depend on a new governor and Congress, so a V-reversal is harder.

There is a flipside. The same Democratic wave that threatens the AI buildout also limits Trump’s room to escalate in Iran. A deal is barely priced. Lower oil would mean a less hawkish Fed, and lower rates help long-duration tech the most.

Market Thoughts 6 Nov 2026 - Equities Bloodbath

- At this point, it is quite clear that the trade is over, and has been over for quite some time; Today was the day people decided to *all* rush to the exits in no order whatsoever

- Retail momo was the first to go a few months ago, with Space stocks and Quantum all crashing. Then now is the time for semis. 80% of the S&P has been in a bear market the past few months; the 20% are now joining them.

- In general, the way I see it now is that it has all been one giant liquidity cycle; In a K-shaped world, money flows to the top 20% of assets that keep the game going, and in this case, it was all in AI; now that the music has stopped, money is flowing out and getting destroyed. 

- This comes after the fact that the Fed has started a new hiking cycle, you have rising costs of living, a war that hasn't stopped and is devastating for the real economy, and it's all now showing up in real time through a blue sweep in midterms

- But of course, the present is already priced in. Now all that's left is what's next. Sadly this sorts of demand destruction is incredibly hard to recover from - you need time. Now that everyone is poor again, you'll need time for some of these assets to bottom out

- I believe that there are certain sectors that are also still forming rounded tops - financials being one; so in general over the next few weeks / months we should be seeing more down moves. 

- Is the AI trade dead though? As assets bottom out, it would be obvious to start picking your horses for the eventual success of the buildout. I do think this is true, but it's going to take time to show who genuinely wins. As the cost of intelligence becomes cheaper and cheaper, it's pretty clear that the whole "infrastructure wins because volume explodes" also isn't as good of an explanation anymore as infrastructure gets better and better. Gun to my head, the winner of better intelligence would instead be the companies that learn to leverage this intelligence into real world outcomes instead (e.g Biotech)

- What's the next trade? It looks pretty grim now, for most sectors. At times like this, it's much better to let the market show its hand, but if you really want a decisive answer, going by the charts, digital assets still look the best - although this has been said for the 20th time; 

- Somehow, every week there is a new "maximally bearish" event and Bitcoin fails to break below 76k. Even if it does break, I have a feeling it's going to fake-out and reclaim. 

- But from a fundamental standpoint there seems to be no good reason for digital assets to do well. So far, most investors I've asked have backward looking indicators that would justify a pump in hindsight, but doesn't necessitate any sort of buying pressure now. Examples include: 4 year cycle lows, relative strength to equities, or cheap fundamentals 

- I will say that the most bullish case I can think of is that akin to software, digital assets are uniquely situated in how they can leverage AI to build more economical output much quicker. In a time where the market is starved of any sort of positive catalyst, digital assets are seeing breakneck rates of adoption e.g Druckenmillers investment into Trade[XYZ], tokenization of stocks, equity perps, ICE partnerships, etc. 

- It would be thus incredibly offside if investors didn't allocate 1-2% minimally into what is potentially a new emerging trend in the markets while everything else crashes. The world hates the previous iteration of crypto, but with this new adoption and people waking up to its usecases, price may follow

Overall though, the best thing to do now is probably remain mostly flat, with a small portion of one's book allocated to these new emerging trends. And the larger portion waits until the time is right to allocate into the death knell of some of these assets that will be 10x'es in half a decade.

Why has today been so bad?

You had multiple sell side analysts on Wall Street come out this morning and basically say the same thing, which is that they are starting to believe capex growth will now peak in 2027. This doesn’t mean capex will stop, but the rate of growth for it will peak in 2027.

This means the rate of growth for semi earnings could be perceived as topping as well. 

At the same time, the market doesn’t know if the Fed will continue to be aggressive with their tightening.

Neocloud debt continues to yield higher, with CoreWeave now having yields at 17%. 

The result is a market sell off across the board. Nvidia is down 9%.

No one believes in the future earnings or low P/Es because if datacenters can’t come online, the revenue itself won’t be there to justify the capex.

The bright side is that mean hyperscalers pull back capex and FCF goes positive sooner than expected along with yields eventually coming down due to lack of new AI debt, but that means semis continue to sell off in that scenario. 

Worst day all year for the Nasdaq.

tweets.text:
Many of the most popular AI benchmarks are badly made. The flaws are easy to build in and hard to catch.

“A lot of the really popular benchmarks out there are kind of trash. This is largely because they’re made by people who don’t have expertise in making evals or environments or training data in general.”

“It’s very easy to make a task that seems good on a surface level, but it’s actually unfair in some way, such that it’s a poor test of model capabilities.”

“A lot of people make their tasks harder by making them unfair rather than actually making the task difficult.”

“It’s very hard to figure this out unless you run ten rollouts, look at the transcripts, see why the model failed, and determine manually: was this actually a legitimate failure?”
